---
title: "4 · Text, Images, and Two Ways to Wait"
---

::: {.milestone}
**Block 2** · Learning goals: Put text and images on the screen, for a fixed time or until a keypress.
:::

The wonderful thing about the draw-flip cycle is that *every* stimulus type follows it. Images work exactly like text: swap `TextStim` for `ImageStim`. Before you run the below script, you need some images. Download them here, unzip, and put the `stimuli/` folder **next to your script**:

<a class="btn btn-primary" href="../materials/cogwheel_stimuli.zip" download>⬇️ Download the CogWheel stimuli (zip)</a>

```python
img = visual.ImageStim(win, image='stimuli/stimulus1_L.jpg')
img.draw()
win.flip()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Where Python looks for images"}
`'stimuli/stimulus1_L.jpg'` is a *relative path*: it means "a folder called `stimuli`, sitting next to this script, containing that file." So the one thing to get right is geography: script and `stimuli/` folder side by side in the same place. If an image ever refuses to load, check this first; it's the most common little stumble of the day, and the fix is just moving a file.
:::

## Two ways to wait

After a flip, we decide how long the stimulus stays. There are two fundamentally different answers, and choosing between them is an *experimental design decision*:

```python
core.wait(2)        # the COMPUTER decides: exactly 2 seconds
event.waitKeys()    # the PARTICIPANT decides: waits for a key press
```

::: {.predict-check data-answer="participant computer computer participant" data-accept="participant, computer, computer, participant"}
Who should decide the duration of each of these four screens? Answer `computer` or `participant` for each, in order, on one line: (a) an instructions screen · (b) a feedback screen after a response · (c) a brief fixation cross between trials · (d) a word in a self-paced reading experiment.

::: {.pc-hint data-if-contains="computer participant"}
Start with (a): people read instructions at very different speeds. Who should control when to move on?
:::

::: {.pc-explanation}
`participant`, `computer`, `computer`, `participant`: (a) `waitKeys()`, because people read at different speeds; (b) `wait()`, a fixed, comparable duration for everyone; (c) `wait()`, fixed and short; (d) `waitKeys()`, because the whole point of *self-paced* reading is that the participant controls the pace — the time they take **is** the measurement. More on that in Session 3.
:::
:::

## Try it

Modify your Chapter 3 script: after the *Hello, world!* screen, show **one image** (pick any file from `stimuli/`), participant-paced. Run it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Show the code"}
```python
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), color='black',
                    fullscr=False, checkTiming=False)

text = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hello, world!',
                       color='white', height=0.1)
text.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

img = visual.ImageStim(win, image='stimuli/stimulus1_L.jpg')
img.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

win.close()
core.quit()
```

Note the pattern repeating: prepare, draw, flip, wait. Once per stimulus on screen.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Summary"}
Every stimulus type follows the same cycle: `ImageStim` is `TextStim` with a picture, and image paths are relative to your script (keep them next to `stimuli/`!). After each flip, one design decision: `core.wait()` when the *computer* should control the duration, `event.waitKeys()` when the *participant* should. One prepare-draw-flip-wait per screen.
:::

**Image on screen, dismissed by your keypress?** Wonderful! Next: [loading all the stimuli at once](05_glob.qmd).
